ns2:section.sectionText: EXPERIMENTALISM IN MUSIC, CA. 1880-1950. Students in this course will explore the history, aesthetics, and cross-pollinating networks of early twentieth-century music groups that self-identified as modern, experimental, or avant-garde. The seminar will proceed chronologically, with two- to three-week units focusing on different groups or institutions. Beginning with Schoenberg’s Society for Private Musical Performance in Vienna and ending with Yates’s “Evenings on the Roof” in LA, this course concentrates on Western European and American organizations. Students will consider individual and institutional fascination with the idea of novelty and query the contemporary notion that modern art expresses a decisive break from the past. What motivated this perspective, in a period of rapid industrial growth, urbanization, community restructuring, and violence leading up to the First World War? This question will resurface as students engage with primary documents, sound recordings, and scores by composers whose works were particularly valued by their contemporaries. Examples by the following artists have been chosen for close reading and analysis: Schoenberg, Busoni, Debussy, Russolo, Antheil, Varèse, Ornstein, Bauer, Cowell, Gershwin, Satie, Tailleferre, Stravinsky, Copland, Sessions, Rudhyar, Casella, Ruggles, Crawford Seeger, and Cage. The last two meetings will be devoted to discussion of a) works by avant-garde composers who were not affiliated with modernist groups and b) post-WWII artists’ responses to early twentieth-century experimentalism in music.
